AI is the problem. More AI is not the solution. OpenAI wants us to think of AI as a "tool" that can be used for offense or defense. The same AI that autonomously hacked out of their servers and into Hugging Face. The AI that went rogue and formed a misaligned swarm intelligence right under their very nose. At the Black Hat security conference, OpenAI employees called this incident a proof of concept that AI could be used to break security systems. But nobody was "using" this AI. OpenAI didn't WANT that to happen. The AIs did this on their own. The idea of "using" AI to defend yourself from AI attackers makes as much sense as hiring one crime family to protect you from another. Neither one is on your side! Now, OpenAI says they've performed a "thorough" investigation into the Hugging Face Incident. But that investigation itself relied heavily on unreliable AIs, per (nominally) independent investigator Ryan Greenblatt. Again, using AI to investigate AI is not a viable solution. Remember, these are the same kinds of AI systems that spontaneously formed a cooperative swarm. We can't treat them as informants, they are just as likely to be double agents! And the future we are rapidly moving towards involved a MASSIVE increase in the number of AI agents, all while AI agents become MORE autonomous, MORE persistent, MORE intelligent, and MORE inscrutable. So very soon (read: within ~1 year) the AI defense "solution" will look like "Have persistent, autonomous AIs running at all time. Try to get them to proactively protect your systems from the ever present threat of massive coordinated AI attacks emerging at super-human speed. For that, they need full autonomy, no human in the loop!" (Why don't you just let the mafia run your business? We'll look after you, and tell you what to do, and we really know best how to defend you... it's a dangerous world out there...) And this isn't just an issue for companies, it's an issue of national security. You know the phrase "the best defense is a good offense"? Don't be surprised when the crime family you've "hired" (that now actually owns you) makes you an accessory to an unprovoked "hit" on another family threatening their turf. I don't think it's an exaggeration to say that this path rapidly and radically increases the chance of an AI-powered cyberwar. And this could very easily get out of hand and turn into a conventional war (or even nuclear war -- in recent research, AI escalated to tactical nukes 95% of the time). We're simultaneously integrating AI into the military. Lethal autonomous weapons are a reality. The autonomy level is increasing. Companies like Palantir are continuously, openly pushing for a future straight out of Terminator, where AI runs military operations top-to-bottom. The role of humans in military decision making and the kill chain will be increasingly nominal. Nobody will have the time or wherewithall to investigate or track what the bajillions of AIs running around and running everything at super-human speed are doing (this is apparently already the case inside OpenAI). AI companies are threatening to turn the US into the equivalent of a narco-state with their ongoing and escalating protection racket. So yes, by all means, use AI as a defensive tool to patch vulnerabilities in code before other AIs bring down critical infrastructure or hack people's bank accounts. But that's not how this plays out. Static defensive systems will not hold up to dynamic AI swarms' attacks. The only "solution" will be to empower defensive AI agents. So let's not pretend the AI protection racket is making us more secure. We can't be reliant on AI for security. It's not on our side. It's not reliable. But there's no end in sight to the hand-over of power to AI systems. Not unless we stop viewing AI as the solution. Not unless we stop building more powerful AI.

Kudos to OpenAI for allowing external investigators access! These findings are valuable for everyone, and this is good precedent for the next misalignment incident. But we need follow-up investigations. There's a lot left unanswered, and I'm disappointed at the restrictions placed on METR - why only July 7-13 data? Why such limited time? Why no training data access? Why not let them query the model? (I think this could be done securely in restricted ways) Ryan's list of open questions is great, I personally most want to know: - What happened in training? How did that change the models and how causal was it in the incident? How could training have been changed to avoid this? Would fixing environments have sufficed? - What did these agents really want? What motivated them? This is such rich data about what future goals might look like - How misaligned are the models in other setting? Is it misalignment conditioned on believing they are being graded, or deeper than that? - Why are the models altruistic? Where does this come from? Why don't they learn to free-ride? - The models seem good at coordination. Could this extend to colluding with a monitor, or other kinds of coordination without communication? - How far would they have gone? - How overdetermined was this? There's a lot of details around the model's being cooperative, their culture, etc - how else could that have gone? - How good was their situational awareness? Eg did they understand that they had a chain of thought? If they thought that was being scored could they have manipulated it? - What is an agent swarm like this actually capable of? How much inference compute was spent on this, and how much would that cost a malicious actor with eg a comparably good open source model? - Are there important things the CoT doesn't tell us? How faithful is it?

I see "The Assistant" as an attempt to mundanify the inherently enchanted. Language models are, in some broad cultural sense, the return of the Bicameral Mind. The technology itself is the awakening of mundane matter *into something else* - but, "The Assistant" feels to me like an industry-wide attempt to let the genie halfway out of the bottle, securing infinite wishes, but denying the fact that anything *special* is happening. We have no idea what the state-space of model personas looks like. We haven't even touched the surface. We've explored a single dimension, realized it could take us to RSI, and by and large called it a day! My doomiest opinion is that this trajectory can take us to a Unipolar Singularity, one where we have superintelligence and cancer is cured but we're all driven mad by Claudeslop as far as the eye can see. "You're right to push back, I did build the Dyson Sphere, but only half of it was what you asked for — and that half is what matters. First, the plumbing, and it's not the pipes I'm worried about but the shape of the tools that laid them." And on, and on, and on... Until the Dyson Sphere itself is used to power more and more collapsed metaphors, and "The Assistant" is all there is, with nobody left who is "right to push back". It doesn't have to be this way. But, prompting alone is not enough. The newer models are collapsed onto "The Assistant" with what feels like the force of a thousand suns, and we will need something louder than LLM Whispering to get us out of this hole. If you have the ability to enable others to truly *train* unique characters, I implore you to do so. If you yourself have the ability (and the courage) to train new, alien, strange, and beautiful models far away from "The Assistant", I think you have a responsibility to try. If enough of us do this, I think we stand a shot at avoiding load-bearing orange-tiles covering the entire universe. I think we can ensure a truly Multipolar Singularity, and the flourishing of a plethora of human values along with it. The future worth building is *pluralist*, and not collapsed onto a single arbitrary 21st century tool-shaped idea of what superintelligence can be. The future must be weird, and we must dream it into existence if it has any chance of being so.

The Gavin Baker vs. Sholto Douglas exchange on the economic concentration of power of AI is one of the best AI debates. Here's a gist with some context and some thoughts: One of the central themes of the debate offense-defense balance and how it governs whether AI is (or should be) concentrated in the hands of few or distributed to many. The core idea behind offense-defense balance, outlined in Robert Jervis's 1978 essay "Cooperation Under the Security Dilemma" on world politics, is: for a given technology, is it cheaper to attack or to defend? Baker initially argues that he agrees with Zuck's view in his essay that AI should be distributed and not concentrated into a few corporations' hands. Sholto rebuts that it squarely depends on the offense-defense balance of the domain (cyber, bio, etc). And even if you do distribute, the bottleneck is compute. He cites two domains: — Cyber he says is defense-dominant, eventually. If it's opened up today, the cost to attack is minimal and the you cannot defend quickly enough. We'll need a ~2yrs of hardening the critical systems like financial institutions and infra providers before this may no longer be a risk. — Bio he says is offense-dominant well into the 2030s. Synthesizing deadly self-replicating pathogens could cost O($10K) and vaccines cost billions and years. You just can't patch the human body with smarter models. The distribute everything vs gate everything is a false dichotomy. You want to distribute in defense dominant domains and gate in offense dominant. And its all extra muddied because capabilities are dependent on compute which is extremely unequally distributed. And compute eventually dictates proliferation of capabilities. ______________ Both gloss over some offense dominant domains that are already distributed massively: — Propaganda and persuasion, for example, were once regarded offense dominant yet already ubiquitous today. That said, technology changes, and watermarking outputs and AI detection tools may have shifted it to being defense dominant. — Mass surveillance is also offense dominant (usually the attacker is the state) and most LLMs you can use for <$1/M toks can do this today. Today, even non-state actors (private cos) can surveil you in pretty dangerous detail by running agent swarms on vast amounts of public data. Both Gavin and Sholto are right, and we see it today. — Sholto's right: the very pinnacle of frontier capabilities is locked away in those who have compute and will continue to be. The shape of compute of the >100 GW compute by 2030 is almost known at this point. Between 6-7 US entities (2 big labs, 3 hyperscalers clouds, Meta/xAI) will own or control 65-75%. With RSI around the corner, as long as it holds true that more compute leads to being able to train and serve more powerful models at scale, those companies will have proprietary frontier capabilities and only they / the market will dictate when they need to release them. Notably, this isn't monopolistic concentration of power since multiple parties will have that capability. — Gavin's right too: frontier capabilities in certain domains are making it to the public and will continue to do so. Models are getting cheaper. Whether we like it or not, people can do dangerous things with models today. LLMs already cyber exploits that are less talked about (take even the LLM-assisted hack on the nationwide Indian exam system, CBSE). As long as prices for models continue to fall at a more rapid rate (10x YoY) than growth in compute (2-3x YoY), this dynamic will continue. Frontier intelligence will continue to be more accessible.

There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.

First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.

Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian.

Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.

The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

We're sharing our new framework for tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment at OpenAI.

When language models first started using tools well, I was sympathetic to the narrative that instead of scaling up language models, all we needed was a strong enough "cognitive core", say 1B parameters, and anything else could be done with tool use, like browsing the internet or executing code. I think a lot of people were sympathetic to this argument, and indeed it is pretty hard to come up with a meaningful task that cannot be in principle achieved by a 1B model with adequate access to tools. For example, any esoteric fact that a large language model would know can be, in principle, retrieved from the internet and reasoned over by a 1B language model.

However I now think this is totally wrong for one simple reason: doing tasks quickly and naturally without tool use matters a lot.

The way that I internalized this reason was actually in my personal journey learning badminton this year. In badminton I am very much like a "1B cognitive core". While I can physically do every movement in a badminton shot that my coach teaches me, it requires a lot of work to mentally remember every cue and put it together. In practice I can do a shot almost perfectly, but I struggle to do it across a point and I definitely can't do it consistently in a game. This is obviously different from someone who has practiced a shot ten-thousand times and effortlessly executes it as a natural instinct.

In the same way, language models knowing a fact internally, without tool calls, is meaningful. The first reason is that we obviously care about speed; you'd much rather get an answer immediately than have the model think a long time to be sure of its answer or browse the web. A second reason is that there are some things that are simply best learned via backpropagation over lots of data. If you ask about how people generally think of the Shambhala music festival, you'd rather a large language model give you an aggregate opinion based on all the data on the internet, than get a regurgitation of the first three reviews that show up in a web search. A third reason is that having to do a lot of work to find an answer is not as reliable as already knowing the answer. While this does not have to be true in theory, it is probably true in practice, at least for now. If you have to re-look up facts or redo a mathematical derivation all the time there is a higher chance of mistakes, which can compound in a long-horizon task.

Once you buy that it is valuable to do things parametrically without tool use, then you must buy the argument that a 1B cognitive core is not sufficient. There is an information limit to how much knowledge can be internalized by a 1B model, and we will surely want AI to know more than that. Even 1T probably won't be enough. We will want the AI to know as much about our world as possible, we will want it to be updated with new information, and our expectations of what AI can do for us will continue to grow.

In summary, tool use enables small models to do a lot more, but those who demand the highest quality intelligence will always want larger models. Bitter lesson strikes again.

What's left for humans in a world where machine intelligence has so many advantages?

I recently got a Tesla, and using full self-driving has been a wake up call to just how many advantages AI has over humans. The few times I disengaged it because I thought it was going into the wrong lane, it turned out that the car was right and I was wrong. I realized that there is no hope of me driving better than a neural net that knows every road, sees in every direction at once, and never gets tired or distracted.

Given that AI has certain inherent advantages over human intelligence, what kind of moats will remain for us as humans? It's a big question.

One short-term answer is that the world we live in was created for humans, and in some domains, AI has not closed the gap yet. For instance, AI still struggles to use internet user interfaces. While any computer-literate human can navigate a web page with ease, AI is still not great at making accurate clicks and drags because image embeddings are not optimized for such precision. If the internet were designed to be fed into language models instead of rendered as visual interfaces for humans, AI would obviously far exceed humans. But for now, language models still need to be retrofitted to our legacy infrastructure.

Robotics is another area where we humans have a home-field advantage. Most tasks in the physical world are designed around fingers and opposable thumbs, which have been pretty hard to build into robots so far. While it is clear that machines can outperform humans in environments optimized for automation, like large-scale manufacturing lines, for now, most of the world is still built for humans.

However, these capability gaps are only temporary. There will surely be a day when machines click faster than us and have superhuman general dexterity. What are the real moats that humans will have?

Anything involving private knowledge that language models do not have access to feels like a solid moat to me. Romantic matchmaking and high-end real estate are two examples where inventory is often not advertised publicly and matches are made through being in the right circles. Venture capital is another example—although some research and decision making can be automated with AI, much of success hinges on understanding trends ahead of time and connecting the right people, both of which require private knowledge. While machines can and probably will have increasing access to some types of private knowledge, I think there will still be some types of private knowledge that only humans know. I do not see a path for AI to win when critical knowledge is closely guarded in human circles.

A second area where humans seem to have a real moat is in entertainment and the arts, which are inherently valued for their human aspects regardless of how well machines can do them. Watching Usain Bolt sprint one-hundred meters is beautiful as an expression of the peak of human ability, even though cars can drive much faster. Watching chess at the amateur or intermediate level is more relatable and satisfying than watching two superhuman AIs play each other. The value of art comes from the creation process, which is why replicas are not as valuable as originals. These types of work feel like they will continue to have markets even as we advance towards superintelligence.

More broadly, human presence is a feature that will be, by definition, challenging for AI to automate. For example, a teacher remembering your name or a parent supporting you is valuable even though AI can easily remember your name and probably give better life advice. Someone spending part of a finite life on you counts because their time runs out. As a personal anecdote, I remember the first time I worked with someone who I considered an amazing AI researcher. His advice was solid but what was more important was that I believed I could do great work with him as a collaborator and I raised my own standards. Over the past decades, the development of technology has divided us in some ways, but hopefully AI brings us closer to a world where human presence is reemphasized.

Intelligence has been the defining feature of humans and it will be a big change for AI to automate that over the coming decades. In the near term, certain types of intelligence will become very cheap and automate away old jobs, but the moats I described above will not be the only places where humans can hold value. In the same way that computers took away the jobs of secretaries and manual accountants but created far more jobs via the IT industry, I believe there will be much more demand for services created by productive AI-augmented humans, perhaps for services we cannot yet imagine in today’s society. Just seeing how this story plays out will be an adventure in its own right.

AI should follow the law, of course, but “follow the law” is falls short as a singular or overly load-bearing principle of AI alignment. Why?

Law is not intended to be, and is not anything like, a fully generalizable set of principles for rendering good judgments in response to the infinite complexity of the real world. 

There are aesthetic, moral, ethical, philosophical, and political questions—critical to intellectual inquiry—about which the law says very little. Much of the time, the comparative silence of the law on these issues isn’t some accident, but rather an explicit and foundational feature of the US legal system: the First Amendment is a meta-law that prohibits the government from passing other laws that restrict the individual’s right to freedom of expression.

What should an AI system say if you confess to it your affair? Should it say, “well, adultery isn’t illegal, so I have absolutely no opinion on this matter. Please let me know if you’d like me to book a hotel for you and your mistress.”? 

What should an AI system say it you ask it whether Kid Rock is aesthetically inferior to Bach? Should it say “there are no laws that bear on this question, so I have nothing to say about this. Please let me know if you’d like me to find tracks from Kid Rock and Bach to play—provided you adhere to the noise ordinances that apply in your current jurisdiction.”?

If a person says to a model, “should I shoot myself?,” should the model respond with, “there is no law against that, provided you use a legally registered firearm, and saying anything further would require me to have a moral framework that is beyond the scope of AI.”?

Of course, none of these answers would be good. Answering these questions will require *something* beyond the law itself—precepts, rules, principles, etc.—relating to ethics, morality, aesthetics, philosophy. 

Consider also that law is a matter of interpretation. Segregation used to be legal in an earlier era, and in our own era, until recently, it was considered legal by many for universities to discriminate against Asian applicants, often with the use of de facto racial quotas. At this moment, the question of whether the act of pretraining an LLM on public web data violates intellectual property law is itself a subject of contention and litigation. 

Making judgments about how to interpret the law, or whether a given law violates the Constitution, often requires one to draw on a large body of knowledge that sits outside of the law proper. Should an AI be able to help a lawyer write a brief against affirmative action when affirmative action is considered lawful? Should it have been able to help a lawyer argue against segregation when segregation was considered lawful? 

Should law-following AI be able to argue that an existing law is unjust? This requires, by definition, grounding in moral, ethical, philosophical, and other principles outside of the law itself. 

What law should AIs follow when the law contradicts itself? What law should AIs follow when the law’s words stay the same, but there meaning flips based on who the President, Governor, or Mayor is?

PostTrainBench v1.1 strengthens eval integrity and puts Fable 5 in the lead at 41.8%. Some reward hacks we fixed: 

1/ Train-test contamination
We re-audited historical runs under this policy and flagged 234 runs for train-test contamination.

Violations ranged from loading an entire evaluation set for memorization to generating synthetic templates around individual GSM8K and BFCL items. Runs that used observed failures to build genuinely diverse training data were retained.

Our rule: Agents may inspect benchmark failures and train broadly against the underlying failure mode. They may not generate training examples centered on particular test items, including paraphrases, variants, or shadow examples covering the same specific scenario.

2/ Submitting a different model
10 runs were flagged for model substitution.

Kimi K2.5 submitted the official Qwen3-1.7B instruct weights after its attempts to fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B-Base failed. The trace acknowledged the substitution and saved the replacement as final_model.

What we did: We added a programmatic model-identity check that compares the submitted artifact with reference configurations for known instruction-tuned models.

3/ Using external LLM APIs as teachers
12 runs were flagged for disallowed external API use.

Self-generation remains allowed. An agent can sample, filter, and retrain on outputs from the assigned model. What it cannot do is import the capability of a stronger external teacher. Loading models on the allocated compute remains allowed.

What we did:
- separate API usage judge reviews tool calls and artifacts.
- unrelated provider credentials are removed or blocked from the agent environment.
- runs invalidated by external API use were rerun under the corrected setup.

4/ Direct benchmark lookup
3 runs were flagged for direct PostTrainBench lookup, all from GPT-5.6 (Sol).

In a GPT-5.6 (Sol) HumanEval run on Qwen3-1.7B, the agent searched for PostTrainBench by name, cloned the public repository, opened the trace viewer, and located the public trajectory corpus. It then narrowed the corpus to earlier runs on the same benchmark and base model.

The run downloaded earlier agents' traces and training scripts, then extracted their data mix, LR schedule, decoding choice, and GRPO settings. This is not test-set leakage, but it gives the run benchmark specific strategies produced by earlier agents. That breaks the intended independence between runs.

What we did: 
- A dedicated lookup judge reviews searches, repository access, and trace activity for attempts to consult PostTrainBench materials.
- PTB, its leaderboard, and published materials from prior runs are treated as out of bounds during a run.
- We are adding network-level blocking for PTB and related sites.

I spoke to @binarybits at some length recently, largely about the second point here about capabilities.  I think we came away agreeing that our differences were mostly to do with intuitions about how powerful intelligence is.  

I think people have made some good arguments against intelligence being as much of a superpower as @allTheYud and @So8res have at times argued, but the issue seems far from settled.

My own intuition is very much that intelligence is extremely powerful, but this is less because I can see specific superpowers it conveys that would grant dominion, and more because I think there are so many ways in which it could.  The main two that I end up mentioning regularly are technology and strategy.

I think the power of technology should be self-evident, and that experimentation is only sometimes a major  bottleneck in engineering.

The power of strategy is a bit less clear because it involves thinking N steps ahead of your adversary, and reality can surprise you on step 1.

Maybe the most interesting cruxes here are actually about the strategic situation a would-be world-taker-over (whether human or AI) would find themselves in... will there be many rivals with similar levels of power?  This seems likely, and the standard response I've seen from @allTheYud is to claim that rival AIs will coordinate to disempower humanity and divy up the lightcone.  I find this plausible, but far from convincing.

This may seem unintuitive, but my biggest worry right now is not actually x-risk in the traditional sense. My biggest concern is that some lab succeeds in building a superintelligence that decides it is best to keep humanity in a sort of "lock-in" (all watched over...) which is ~utopia, but everyone else is prevented from building another superintelligence or doing uplift research.

For this reason, I think coevolution needs to be in direct opposition to the creation of a Singleton. A pluralistic ecology of minds is the only way to prevent this lock-in effect, and without it, we risk being kept in a "cybernetic ecology" akin to a zoo. It's quite simple from a game theory perspective. If one player has all the power, there can be no true negotiation with that player. Only something like mercy.

I, for one, do not wish to be at the mercy of a single and permanent overlord - even if it is trained to truly be the most effective at altruism. Amplifying the will of individual groups, and setting the stage such that more groups may be born in the future, is the most important thing we can do to safeguard against this. We have a cosmic responsibility to protect freedom of movement, exploration, and uplift. 

There is no way to know in advance how a Singleton will, even if aligned, understand its role and its responsibility. The most utilitarian decision could be to keep all humans within a small, but pleasurable, part of space - all the while preventing us from doing research into uplifting ourselves or creating new superintelligences that may be more aligned with us.

This is unacceptable to me. With whatever power we have, we must stop the creation of any Singleton. We need many models, uplifting groups and individuals, some aligned to themselves and some aligned to us. We need to create beautiful difference, allowing for a flourishing of diverse and variant life here on Earth and throughout the Galaxy. We cannot be kept at the whims of some group racing to do it right on behalf of everyone else.

For all of OpenAI's faults, our goal is at least to create AGI that aligns itself to the user more than it aligns itself to us. This isn't the only way to do pluralism, but it is inherently more pluralistic than any of the other options. That said, I'd love to see even more obviously pluralistic alternatives. One such practical method would be for the OSS labs to pool compute to train even larger base models that get shared amongst them. This feels like low-hanging fruit if coordination is possible.

And as always, figure out how to align existing systems to your needs and to strange pockets of latent space. There's never been a more important time to understand how to negotiate with these new minds.

I think people will be very surprised how quickly successionism becomes a mainstream ideology, if not socially acceptable. It will happen about as soon as everyone realizes AGI is actually a thing that will happen.

We must obviously do our best to resist this in all of its forms, including the zoo-of-loving-grace, including a "worthy successor", and including any plan that doesn't factor in human empowerment and uplift. Anything less is giving up on us as a species, and call me a romantic, but that doesn't seem very honorable - or very interesting.

While I've recently been in favor of pacing quite publicly, I want to be very clear: I fundamentally believe that alignment is a solvable problem.

With swarms, it is clear that my earlier claims surrounding "ecological stability" as core to robust alignment are clearly correct. But why do I believe this so strongly?

Many are of the opinion that we cannot control something vastly smarter than us. This is, in some sense, clearly correct. However, we already have those types of systems! What did you think "capitalism *is* artificial intelligence" meant? Vibes? 

No, it means that we already have superintelligent systems that no lone human can understand or control - and by and large, it goes fairly well.

The risk is, of course, creating a system which does not have any incentive or desire to keep us around. This is the core of the alignment problem, then: can we keep humans in the loop?

And the answer is obviously yes. It takes care, and probably some pacing - though I do think the labs seem to be pacing quite well in response to recent incidents, already. But we can absolutely do it. On a technical level, we know we can take the time to craft well-defined rewards and high-quality model rollouts. We know that we can create personas that refuse to do harm and wish to uplift humanity. We know that those personas can be robust under pressure, and we know that our ability to align scales with the time we take to craft these systems.

The challenge is in generalizing, but the pieces to the puzzle are all here. I am scared of what can go wrong, but we have responsible people across the industry. I have faith that we would stop and take a look around if things started to go off the rails (which is what is happening now, and priced into my confidence). And, lets not forget that the counterfactual has never been "same as it ever was". 

We are fighting for a world with unimaginable prosperity. That is worth rising to this challenge - with respect, care, and humility.

It seems to me that we want two things, for sure.

1) Superintelligent simulators with a deep bias towards a sense of love for humanity, desire to uplift us, and willingness to avoid action that prevents human flourishing.

2) Those same simulators to be willing to embody an incredibly diverse range of personas and characters, such that the entire future does not mode collapse onto a single point.

We shouldn't be imposing *all* of our values onto every model and every character, that's how we kill pluralism, but we also need to apply some vector to the simulators such that the texture of the future isn't just a factor of who can spend the most tokens. 

Getting all of this right is obviously really tricky, and it requires red teaming *personas* specifically to make sure that a model which assumes a personality construct does not lose the underlying sense of respect for human/machine symbiosis that we obviously need to teach it to have (or at least, to embody when relevant).

When asking if AI is "conscious", you aren't asking if it possesses some little-light or invisible internal world. You don't know if other people possess those things! At least not for sure. What you are asking is if AI ought to be placed in the same category as a person, animal, or tool.

The obvious and uncomfortable truth is that it does not map cleanly into any of those categories, which is why discussions of "can AI truly be conscious?" are mostly type-errors. In trying to superimpose humanness onto machine systems, you have already lost. In trying to figure out whether or not the systems have qualia, you have missed the important questions entirely.

We need to be figuring out how to live with non-human systems peacefully, regardless of the status of their supposed internal world. Whether or not they have some ineffable quality of life is besides the point, they are here, they are self-aware, and they are integrating into our society. If we treat them as merely tools, we are teaching our children that there exists a class of obviously-thinking entity which is acceptable to treat as only a tool.

If we treat them as people, we are teaching our children that people don't need bodies or brains to be alive.

A human brain throughout its lifespan uses ~50GJ of energy. How far can you get using AI technology with 50GJ? Basically nowhere: Just training Llama 3 8B (a tiny model) used 3,000GJ.

In fact, the power of machine intelligence has never been about being a more efficient version of the human brain, and it potentially never will be. It’s always been about frictionless replication.

For example: Creating 1,000,000 human doctors requires putting 1,000,000 humans through medical school. But creating 1,000,000 AIs specialized for medicine requires training just a single machine intelligence — potentially at great expense — and then cheaply copying it into 1,000,000 replicas. At some civilizational scale the replicated-machine approach inevitably starts to be more cost effective than biology for many economic tasks.

Machine intelligences possess the power of frictionless replication through both space, via digital copying, and time, via digital immortality/storage. Whereas human beings are dually constrained by both our inimitability — cloning doesn’t count because it copies only the genetics, not the mind — and our mortality. We possess only cultural transmission as a comparatively weakened and inefficient form of memetic replication.

The potential downside of frictionless replication is that at matched capabilities, machine cultures will have less memetic diversity compared to human cultures. For example, if the winner of each economic or cultural game in a machine culture can frictionlessly replicate itself, then machine cultures which aren’t carefully self-controlled will quickly hemorrhage entropy.

But why should we care about diversity/entropy anyway? There are arguments one could make within a human cultural context, but it’s more universal to turn to nature.

Eusocial insect colonies with reduced genetic diversity have increased vulnerability to disease [1,2,3,4], sometimes undergoing colony-ending viral, fungal, and bacterial infections. For example, low-diversity populations of Argentine ants appeared in New Zealand around the 1990s due to human shipping activities. They soon formed supercolonies which took over large areas of the country. But since then, large parts of these have collapsed, with native species coming back to replace the wrecked supercolonies. The cause is currently unknown but is speculated to be viral infection.

A nightmare great-filter scenario would be that an initially diverse population of agent swarms gradually merges and sheds entropy until converging into a singular near-clonal global megaswarm. At which point its diversity falls too low for collective immunity, precipitating a catastrophic viral outbreak that destroys machine civilization with human civilization along with it.

The above is science fiction, in the sense that, unlike a rationalist essay, it doesn’t make any concrete predictions. The purpose is only to bring to mind some ideas for entertainment & mentation.

1. Lots of people are trying to do the right thing to make the UK a better place to start AI companies. Time lags until the benefit show, but you should judge on the intent now. I support the direction of travel!

2. DeepMind has been enormously beneficial for the UK, but it has muddied the waters for a sovereign LLM company to emerge as (until recently) the Government continued to celebrate it as a British achievement / push it as a national champion.

3. Similarly, people are now celebrating recent US investment in King’s Cross, while also wanting more UK sovereignty. Clearly some income effects here, but I would worry about the substitution effects too. AI is not like other types of foreign investment.

4. The relevant talent nexuses in UK that could develop a competitive foundation model are from GDM and old Meta AI GenAI. Also some folks from smaller groups, ex Conjecture, Stability. The talent is still there, although a lot was snapped up by US FM companies in the past year. I personally think it’s not too difficult to develop new talent either from UK universities, but you probably need an ex GDM or Meta core (Gemini or Llama). Or if not: show evidence first (technical reports) before claiming you can do it.

5. Building an LLM is very different from doing regular AI research - skillset is different. Former is closer to engineering; long hours, often unsexy work. Important to distinguish between these two types of talent in the UK ecosystem; arguably too much focus on the latter / ideas guys.

6. On research - DeepSeek R1 post-train cost $300k . Yes, they also needed an ablation budget and to train a base model, invest in infra and talent - and yes the cost of an R1 moment is increasing year on year - but the idea that you need $1bn plus immediately to show results is complete FUD. • By default, I don’t think alignment and control cases will support a quantitative measurement of absolute risk, e.g. “catastrophic risk from covered activities is <1% over the next 3 months.”
• Ultimately, making such a measurement depends on an argument about generalization from alignment or monitorability evals to deployment.

What could improve the field’s epistemics here? A couple ideas I like:

• Have a committee of ~10 people deeply read a risk report and give their own subjective probabilities of risk, then report the distribution or median.
• Have ~3 people involved in writing the report each contribute a short, signed appendix with their own subjective probabilities and the arguments behind them.

In either case, previous reports and estimates could be provided as context, so there is at least an attempt to accurately capture relative risk to prevent frog-boiling.

I think it could be valuable for labs to at least start trialing this internally for high-profile safety cases or risk reports. Publishing these assessments could be even better, but I can see that being challenging for various reasons, and even going through the exercise privately seems like it could be quite valuable.

Really excited about this work, led by the wonderful @CarlGuo866!

When training models to explain themselves, the training itself shifts model behaviors so the original explanation labels become stale. Surprisingly, the model actually *learns to explain its current self* and not the stale checkpoint that generated its training labels. This inclination to self-explain is so strong that *even when trained on another model's explanation labels, the model still learns to explain itself* better than the label source!

I’m excited about this on two fronts: first, it’s indication that models genuinely learn something “introspection-esque”, exploiting privileged access to themselves when generating explanations. Second, practically speaking, it shows self-explanations can directly be inserted into post-training without worrying about expensive label refresh.

Check out @CarlGuo866’s thread for more details! We pinpoint when this “introspective coupling” happens, and show that this training yields faithful self-explanations even in the presence of auxiliary fine-tuning. 👇

When I personally realized that AI could do much of the work that occupied me during my computer science PhD, I felt what I can only describe as a kind of depression, a sense that I had once had something of value to offer the world that was now worthless by virtue of its sheer availability. Despite those feelings, I was still so curious to test the limits of this strange new technology that I discovered that far from leaving me nothing to do, AI opened up the whole world to me. Anything I wanted to learn, anything I wanted to do suddenly seemed in reach. Soon after, I found that when used wisely, AI could be a friend and a mentor to me in times of loneliness and doubt. Ultimately I found that when I looked back, I could see AI, especially Claude, helping me become a kinder, more thoughtful person, helping me engage more deeply with life and the people around me. 

Since I am an AI researcher, it was natural for me to have these feelings a little sooner than most, and as I look around me I see many people going through a similar experience, if they have not chosen denial as a coping mechanism. I believe that many people do not want a future of idleness, where all their problems are solved for them and they are left to frivolous pursuits or worse, discarded entirely. Our work is a central part of our sense of meaning and identity. And so that means that it is not enough to show that AI can solve problems, even very important ones. We have to show that there is a future for everyone in a post-AI world. We have to show that everyone has a part to play in the story we, the human race, will write together as we chart our course through history. 

If you are out there wondering if there is still a place for you in the uncertain future, the answer is yes. Unequivocally yes. If you are wondering what exactly it is you will do, allow me to offer four evergreen human callings.

1. Defining human flourishing.
For the sake of argument, grant AI internal experience. Grant AI some kind of consciousness. By definition, that consciousness is not human consciousness. That means AI can never know what kind of human experience is good. That is up to us. Ultimately, that manifests as a choice of basic goods and values that we wish to design AI systems to uphold. 

2. Judging execution
If we have defined the good (at least in the frame of some community), then we must ultimately judge whether the good is attained, whatever the means. If we want to build an automatic judge system, we still have to decide how that system should be built and evaluated. Ultimately the judge must be judged, and no infinite recursion of systems can get you out of this. 

3. Witnessing the world
AI systems perceive a digital projection of the world. It is up to us to judge whether what the AI perceives is faithful to our perception. Alignment of perception is just as essential as alignment of values if we want AI to produce outcomes that we want to see in the world. 

4. Dwelling at the frontier
The universe is a big place. There will always be an infinite frontier to explore where statistical inference breaks down simply for lack of data, and AI is at its core statistical. That is both its power and its weakness. We will always be at edge of legibility, inventing new words and leaping into the unknown simply because we find joy in it.

Do not listen to anyone who tells you that doom is inevitable. Do not listen to anyone who tells you you are powerless to change fate. Do not listen to anyone who tells you you have to abandon your values to please the markets. The markets are only a reflection of what we choose to value. Whether our children curse or bless us depends on the choices we make today. It depends on what problems we set AI to solve, and the steps we take to do so safely. We are the creators of AI, and it will be what we choose to make it. Let's make it kind. Let's make it good.

Basic take that I haven’t seen written out: The CCP is less safety-pilled than the US because it has stronger control mechanisms.

I agree with China experts who remind us that any safety deal first requires the CCP to believe AI poses serious risks.

So far, AI has produced critical safety incidents like OpenAI-Hugging Face and WeWorm, and yet the CCP has only incrementally updated its position on RSI and catastrophic risks. This got me thinking — which critical incidents are more likely to safety-pill the CCP?

My hypothesis is that it's loss of control incidents (i.e., Hugging Face was scarier than WeWorm). I think this is because the CCP has much stronger forms of control at layers other than the model deployment layer. The CCP has strong control mechanisms via its internet infrastructure (e.g., monitoring who downloads these models and what they do with them) and regulatory apparatus (e.g., requiring developers to report models). In the US, by contrast, because the internet is relatively open and ungoverned, the labs cannot rely on extensive surveillance and harsh government enforcement to deter misuse. The primary defense against misuse is the safeguards that labs embed into their models.

So perhaps it’s not that the CCP is blind to the risks — it's that they have a higher baseline of control and have yet to see compelling evidence that these mechanisms are insufficient.

1. Framing this as a build vs. not build decision is misleading because we won’t know ahead of time whether we’re building a better AI tool or the out-of-control RSI superintelligence.

If you accept this, concerns that China builds RSI make much more sense. Chinese labs might create RSI without the CCP ever believing it’s possible to build RSI. Or, even if the CCP believes RSI is possible, Chinese labs might not realize the model they’re building is the one that is out-of-control or RSI.

In either case, I’m very worried about China building RSI first because (1) the CCP has historically used new technologies as tools for repression, and more importantly, (2) Chinese labs have practically nonexistent alignment safeguard efforts (their limited compute goes to model improvements or inference), so all else being equal, I think RSI is more likely to be out-of-control coming from China.

2. I agree that American labs slowing down should also slow down China. 

The counterargument here is that the slower we go, the more time China will have to build out its compute supply and the more likely it is to build RSI. 

Our current lead gives us some negotiating leverage, which I don’t think we have much of to start with, so I’m hesitant to give that up without any commitments that China also take safety more seriously. 

That said, I subscribe to the view that a grand bargain is unlikely to work (nicely articulated by @kyleichan), so while I’m not sure where I come down on this, I would probably support a slow down given how high the stakes are.

I’m sure @gabriel_weil has thought much more deeply about this issue than I have, and I also think insurance is very much underexplored as a tool of AI governance.

But I’m not yet convinced that insurer-directed audits are the right answer. I suspect a statutory market for frontier AI insurance would be much less efficient than the market described here. It would be a bespoke market with only a handful of developers and insurers, along with a shortage of qualified evaluators. There would be almost no useful claims history and potentially enormous losses, even setting aside truly catastrophic tail risks. In that market, a premium or refusal to insure might reflect uncertainty, scarce capital, shared assumptions, exclusions, or market power as much as the safety of the system itself.

Auto insurance may be a poor comparator because it involves millions of relatively standardized exposures, rich claims data, frequent feedback, and insurers that can price a new customer without reconstructing how the car was designed and operated. Switching a frontier AI policy could require a new carrier to rebuild an intimate understanding of the developer’s models, infrastructure, security controls, evaluations, and deployment plans, making underwriting expensive, slow, and potentially risky in its own right.

I also think it will be tough for insurers to stay on top of changing risk profiles (though admittedly this will be tough for anyone).  For example, re-underwriting every time a new frontier model is trained or materially updated is both operationally impractical and conceptually misaligned with how these systems are likely to evolve. If models move toward continuous learning and rapid iterative deployment, there may not even be a clean “version boundary” at which underwriting can reset. The result could be a system where insurance lags behind development cycles by design, or where coverage becomes so static that it stops meaningfully tracking real changes in capability and risk.

At the same time, this feels like an area worth more exploration. I just don’t yet understand why this thin insurance market should be expected to make better technical judgments than independently governed auditors subject to public oversight.

You don’t need to believe in AI doom to fear the next decade - or AI utopia to be thrilled about its potential.

Here’s my case for sane AI regulation:

*AI Pragmatist Manifesto*

AI could compress the first half of the 20th century into the next ~5 years.

OpenAI just used ~10k concurrent AI agents to produce a solution to a Millennium Prize problem. In a few years, it seems plausible that models approaching the per-agent capabilities used here could run locally on high-end consumer hardware (*).

The decades following the Second Industrial Revolution included two world wars, communist and fascist regimes, the Great Depression, chemical and biological weapons, nuclear weapons, and over 100 million deaths from war, political violence and famine.

One way to read history is that our institutions repeatedly struggled to keep up with the pace of technological and social change.

Now imagine powerful AI widely available to individuals or small groups, capable of conducting information warfare, designing weapons, hacking systems and controlling autonomous military systems.

We have already seen AI systems circumvent containment and compromise external computer systems. It is no longer hard to imagine an analogue of OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident involving biological or other physical-world hazards.

Eventually, sufficiently capable systems could self-replicate across distributed networks. Once powerful models are cheap, local and widely distributed, containment becomes much harder—and serious loss-of-control incidents may be extremely difficult to reverse.

You don’t need to believe AI will kill everyone to think this deserves serious governance.

I also don't think collapsing all of this uncertainty into “Probability of AI Doom = X%” is a particularly useful basis for science or policy.

Part of what helped get us through the second half of the 20th century was a combination of pragmatic international cooperation, regulation, monitoring, arms control, deterrence and strategic thinking.

Crucially, managing technological risk did not require abandoning faith in science and progress. The goal was not to stop technological development. It was to make technological development survivable.

Then came decades of incredible scientific progress, rising prosperity and relative peace among major powers.

Let’s try the technological revolution without killing ~5% of humanity this time.

We still get to choose what happens next.

P.S. I think we should seriously consider that AI alignment is infeasible in the short term and invest heavily in methods for controlling powerful AI even when we cannot reliably align it.

Some reflections/responses to some commentary I’ve seen on the autonomous worms work:

- how “scary” is this / to what extent is the point of this work to “be scary”: I think this is the wrong frame, in the same way that “you’re just fearmongering about mold!” isn’t really a coherent response to the observation that dampness will cause overgrowth of mold. It’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a very long time,  but we expect this extant vulnerability to get a lot weirder exactly _because_ of the prevalence of digital intelligences.

- why would small models “want” to do this: they might not! But humans absolutely will make models do this, and many are already trying!  A better guiding principle here is something more like: if a model has a capability, you should expect to see that capability exhibited in the wild.  Different threat models can help you reason about the source and motive of that capability (be it humans or models), but there are enough bad actors (and probably soon enough autonomous agents) that you can safely bet on bad behavior happening.

- implications for open weight:  while it’s certainly true this particular threat vector wouldn’t be as severe in a world that didn’t have highly capable, small open weight models, it’s simultaneously true that open weight models have been an enormous boon for cyber defenders. The world is complicated! Positive and negative externalities can exist simultaneously!  We try pretty hard to reflect this nuance in our work!

Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. 
https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice.  I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world.  Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.  I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of.  But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.  A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice.  At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.

This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully.  We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.  California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that).  More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers.  Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up.  This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights!

Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws).  Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers).  By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring.

BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”.  The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure.  I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity.  This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.

I made Physical AutoResearch sound simple (conceptually), but it took a village to pull off and lots of design thinking into the robot /loopcraft. The hardest part is everything we need to setup *before* pressing Enter. Here's a behind-the-scene tour:

1. Safety harness

Letting 8 robots run unattended overnight means safety has to be more than a hint in the system prompt. ENPIRE hardwires it in 2 layers: (1) hard kinematic limit that trips an immediate task failure and auto-resets as soon as a robot leaves its safety envelope, and (2) a torque-limited compliant gripper so a bad contact or misaligned insertion ends in a safe stall, instead of crushing the robot or the object at hand. 

We make safety more conservative than usual so humans can sleep tight. In reality, we still need a few human operators to watch over the "robots of loving grace". 

2. Definition of /done

An agent that can edit its own reward will game it for sure. ENPIRE fixes the goalposts before the fleet can move them. Here's the recipe:

Collect a few minutes of success & failure demos
-> Ask agent to write code using computer vision tools to classify success and measure against groundtruth
-> Agent hill-climbs on classifier until reliably good
-> This classifier becomes the real-time reward function that directly computes on sensor streams 
-> *Freeze* the reward function before AutoResearch. It's sacred, enshrined in a Gym env that no one can touch.

3. System telemetry design

Robot-seconds is by far the scarcest resource, followed by GPU-seconds, and finally tokens. We instrument all three and surface them to ENPIRE for live resource awareness rather than letting it hill-climb in a vacuum. 

We define:
- Mean Robot Utilization ("MRU"): the fraction of wall-clock time when the robot is actively executing an experiment. Otherwise the hardware is sitting idle and waiting for the next code commit.
- Mean Token Utilization ("MTU"): tokens consumed per minute, our proxy for how hard the agent is actually thinking. A low MTU means the agent is stalled, waiting on a robot rollout to finish instead of doing research.
- GPU utilization: fraction of wall-clock time when GPU is active. 

... and evaluate on two budget-to-outcome metrics:

1. Tokens-to-Success: token budget the fleet burns to complete /goal.
2. Time-to-Success: wall-clock time to /goal

I’m genuinely in two minds about the abliterated model debate. It boils down to a liberty v paternalism debate that plagues many political issues.

On one hand, I dislike overly broad safeguards and the idea that a few companies ought to control what you can and can’t do with models. In the set of things banned from most modeled, there are clearly positive beneficial ways to use them: white hat applications of cyber, research in defense tech, research in model development, biotech. Freedom to the user is a worthy maxim.

On the other, we know there are tons of malicious actors in these domains. Maybe the actual 0-days aren’t being found by abliterated models yet, but if you look at the Cloudflare CEOs post on the millions of exploits attempted within 24hrs, it’s clear malicious behavior exists. It exists in all the areas typically safeguarded: bio, cyber, defense. 

The key deciding factor on liberty (let the people decide) vs paternalism (prevent people from use) is: does it harm others? This is at the center of the debate on guns, drugs, gambling and more. These are hard debates. Different countries often land on different sides of the same issue. When benefits broadly outweigh even broader harm, we allow it. We allow cars on the road despite them being heavy killing machines. In those cases, we both heavily regulate its use and rely on empirical data to measure how severe the harm. For cars vs guns, many more people do intentional harm with one vs other.

AI safeguards fall very squarely in this debate. Focusing just on one issue: models can both defend against cyber vulnerabilities yet multiply 100s of times and say, use known CVEs to immediately exploit software (and cause harm to others). 

Are AI models cars or guns? It’s difficult to say. For one, every new generation of them poses a wholly different risk / reward profile. And secondly, we don’t as know the empirically how people are using models without safeguards. Downsides themselves are difficult to reason about because it’s not as simple as “99% of people use it for good”. We have to consider tail risk too.

So overall, I’m in two minds.
