AI will not automate radiologists like you think

We have been talking for years now about AI automating jobs. Radiology has been a prime target, with Geoff Hinton once claiming, “people should stop training radiologists now, it’s just completely obvious that within five years, deep learning is going to do better than radiologists”, which is funny since he said that in 2016. There is now more demand for radiologists than ever, so clearly things did not turn out the way many thought. Here I will make a prediction that while radiology will change in the coming decade, radiologists will not be automated away any time soon. I will use radiology as an example but I think these principles will broadly apply to any field where demand can be elastic and quality can scale with increased intelligence.

First of all, we have seen in the short history of language models that there is a “jagged edge of intelligence”, where AI excels at verifiable tasks with a lot of data but is underwhelming on less common tasks. One thing most AI researchers underestimate about radiology is that it is actually extremely multi-task. There are at least a hundred conditions that can be diagnosed from x-rays alone, and thousands using CT and MRI. AI will first master common and easy-to-see conditions and it will not be as good as experts at less-common diseases just because there is less data for that. This jagged edge will certainly improve over time but this means that AI will certainly be used as a triage tool at first, rather than full automation in one go. I would guess that this process from solid triage tool to full automation would take 3-5 years in the best case scenario, because training AI to get all the edge cases right will be bottlenecked by data collection of rare diseases, and also because radiology isn’t currently a focus for frontier labs.

Second, there will be elastic demand for radiology as it gets cheaper per unit. I think elastic demand (“Jevons paradox”) is the most underrated phenomenon when people think about AI automation. In software, it is obvious that I have way more demand than before because Claude Code makes it so easy. These days I ask Claude Code to build a custom three-thousand line html viewer to help me visualize every little RL run that I do. The same thing will happen in radiology. If there is essentially no cost or latency of interpreting an MRI, a physician can order many scans preemptively to better diagnose a case. So with AI tools, a radiologist might have to read only 20% of inbound scans, but there might be 5x more scans inbound. Many developing countries have fewer than one radiologist per million people and they will also want to send a lot of radiology to be interpreted.

Longer term, cheap and fast radiology interpretation will also drive incentives to build cheaper radiology scanners. If an MRI had essentially no latency for interpretation, medical devices companies will want to build much cheaper MRI machines that can be used more frequently, perhaps even in the middle of a surgery. AI will accelerate the development of scanning technology, too. If a full body MRI was only $100 dollars I would totally want to get one every month instead of every two years. I can imagine a world where people get 10 or 100x the number of scans they do today, largely for preventative care, if radiology were 10-100x cheaper.

Third, even if we did have a model that could outperform the world’s best radiologists today, that would not be the end of all work on radiology. Medicine is a field of change. We may develop new treatment protocols that require reading radiology images in a way that radiologists currently aren’t used to. New scanners may reveal diseases that we cannot currently diagnose today with radiology alone. Some radiologists will change their work from reading scans to doing frontier research to advance our understanding of radiology and translate new knowledge into updated models.

Moreover, I am sure that we will ask for more out of our AI models than ever before. With a good flywheel, we may one day train AI models that can use radiology images to predict disease probabilities far into the future. With good prediction algorithms, cancer may be detected months earlier than we can detect it now. Society will invest a lot into this research and this will contribute even more to increased demand for radiology and the best AI around it.

On top of all of this, the medical system is typically slower to adopt new technology and has more regulation compared to technology companies. There is legacy infrastructure and medical centers need to constantly support patients which makes it hard to integrate new technology. This is even more true in developing countries. Moreover data access tends to be limited due to HIPAA, deidentification, IRBs, etc. So I think radiologists will be in demand for a while.

While some worry about radiology being totally automated, I think there is a more exciting future for radiology than ever before—one where there is more demand and we ask for more predictive power from our intelligence. This is similar to how many of us feel that programming will thrive more than ever before despite drastic change in the field. More generally, any domain where demand can be elastic and quality can scale with increased intelligence will, like radiology, similarly flourish with the development of AI. This is certainly a more exciting and nuanced future than what Hinton described in 2016!

(Finally, to be fair to Hinton, he did acknowledge in a recent podcast that he was wrong and also agrees with the elastic demand argument.)

I'm on board with the broad idea of doing exploratory interpretability with neurons, e.g. neuron-based attribution graphs, for pragmatic problems like why did a model do a sketchy thing? I think this work provides some reasonable evidence, in addition to good earlier work from
Transluce, that this might actually work for practical purposes, and has some advantages over the standard alternatives like SAEs/transcoders. I do not agree with some people's grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering, solving interpretability etc.

I expect that a neuron-based attribution graph will still have significant error and be missing a lot just like transcoders, once you prune them down to the most important components, even if they solve error terms. Which is fine for pragmatic purposes, and may suffice for getting the gist of what's going on, but I remain pessimistic about really fully understanding things and being confident there's nothing we're missing. I do think that using neurons is just vastly easier to, for example, do on a frontier model, which is great. I'm also excited to see more innovation in using agents to interpret neurons. I feel like this is an area the field has somewhat neglected, and where there's probably a very high ceiling on how far things can go. The SwiGLU double negative thing is also a useful point.

I still think superposition is real and this work doesn’t really affect my cruxes. Most importantly, it seems highly likely to be true that the model can represent more concepts in the residual stream than it has dimensions, ie representational superposition, which I think the authors agree with me on. For neuron/computational superposition, it seems to me like language models have far more facts and memorized things in them than they have neurons. And that superposition is an efficient way to pack in more facts than you have neurons by representing them as linear combinations of neurons, especially for arbitrary unstructured values. Facts/memorized content is largely an unstructured database of key-value pairs IMO and I don’t see how this is compatible with a monosemantic view of neurons. I expect that weak neuron activations contain lots of semantic superposition-y info, which, if ablated, would meaningfully damage network performance. As I understand the work, it does not properly address what's going on with weak neuron activations in LLMs (I am skeptical of how much vision results will transfer, eg I expect small image models memorise far less). This picture is compatible with the highest activations of a neuron being mono semantic (though IMO the post defines monosemantic too loosely, I think I’d call a fair few of those polysemantic). It’s also plausible that the most important concepts are likely to correspond to a neuron (or a handful), which would be great, and may suffice for practical purposes!

Similarly, my impression is that SAEs generally don't find things that are a
single neuron, or even very sparse in the neuron basis, and are often a better basis for certain tasks than the neuron basis, though the evidence base is kinda weak here since we largely focus on residual stream or layer output SAEs, I’d love to see work on this in Goodfire’s forthcoming paper! I also think residual stream SAEs are extremely useful, as they give a good bottleneck of the model’s information at this token and layer, and I don’t see a good way to replicate them in the neuron framework.

And kudos to Nick for updating a bunch of his historical vision work! Revisiting old results with modern tools and more rigour seems great.

My top takeaway from assessing Gemini 4: Argon is significantly less monitorable than past models, and IMO this trend is likely to continue, like Sol -> Astra. It can evade a realistic CoT+action monitor to do simple sabotage half the time.

We can reliably maintain control for now, with good CoT monitoring, as it still frequently slips up, but we need to be prepared for when that stops being true in future models, which may be sooner rather than later. Among other things, we really need interpretability methods that can reliably capture unverbalized motivations in models, with minimal hallucinations

I suspect this is driven by the model being highly capable without CoT, being capable of 5.5 arithmetic steps in a single forward pass (4 for Fable, 7 for Astra). It seems to omit information from its CoT more often, though in non-adversarial settings the CoT is still very helpful in practice, and remains in legible English. It still needs CoT to do the hardest tasks, but any given task becomes "easier" with each new frontier model.

It is also highly situationally aware, and shows awareness of the existence of CoT monitors and that it may want to evade them, eg it sometimes decides to avoid terms like "scheming" in the output or to keep its thoughts brief as a result. For now, these concealment strategies are pretty obvious in the CoT, but this suggests future misaligned models may successfully evade CoT monitors.

Fun fact: RLSlow was named after Thinking, Fast and Slow. The idea was that language models already had a kind of "fast" thinking, producing an answer immediately, and that we could use RL to teach them "slow" thinking: deliberate, multi-token reasoning that spends more compute working through a problem.

What I remember most from those days is how early the team developed real conviction in the direction, and how much work went into earning it. We were developing the algorithms, designing careful experiments to test the ideas, and watching the empirical evidence accumulate. These were many long nights babysitting runs, understanding what the results were telling us, and figuring out what to try next. A lot of those early discussions were with Ilya, and later with Jakub.

Pretty early, the evidence had already pushed us to a strong view: RL for reasoning would scale. Models would learn to spend more compute at inference time to reason through increasingly hard problems, and this would fundamentally change how we think about inference. 

Many of us also spent countless hours reading through reasoning traces. Seeing how models arrived at answers, not just the answers themselves, felt like a powerful new lens on generalization and alignment.

These ideas feel obvious now. They really weren’t then.

Tl;dr of my views on AI safety: 

1. My main threat models involves (a) non-state actors asymetrically exploiting cheaper technologies over time (see Bobbitt's 'Terror and Consent'); and (b) the road to state overreach and creeping authoritarianism being paved with good intentions. Misuse, bad engineering, and institutional failure more than alien 'scheming'.

The difficulty of specifying 'alignment' in the abstract + principal-agent problems suggests that engineering system-level boundaries is the way to go. Also ASI is not a joker card, this applies to powerful systems too. 

4. Automating AI R&D is harder than people make it out to be, and does not mean you suddenly lose control. Model gains also remain tethered to bottlenecks, deployment feedback, costs/limited compute, and human normative direction. Humans delegating more does not mean they're out of the loop.

5. AI futurism is too often fatalistic. I disagree that competitive pressures will *necessarily* reduce humans to pets or a sideshow. Automating 'execution' actually pushes humans up the ladder of abstraction toward normative direction and governance; but for the good world we should actively protect and improve liberal democracy.

I will try to explain the 4 critical belief updates from this:

1/ neural networks are not fundamentally unintelligible to humans

It has seemed since the beginning of deep learning that neural networks are in some sense fundamentally unintelligible artifacts.

You throw in massive amounts of compute and parameters and these alien systems somehow find connections in the data that we cannot find ourselves.

But more importantly, these connections seemed not just “difficult to understand” but rather “intelligible in an embedding space higher dimensional that the human embedding space.”

When you look at old interpretability papers (esp. from Nick and Chris Olah, I’m thinking of the old posts on distill pub which I would highly recommend looking at as a precursor to reading Nick’s post today like “Activation Atlas”, “Thread: Circuits” and “Multimodal Neurons in Aritifcial Neural Networks”), you find that inspecting the response patterns of individual neurons and small groups of neurons yield oddly complex psychedelic patterns.

As you go deeper into the network, you find increasingly unintelligible and superhuman response patterns (for example, go to “Activation Atlas” and scroll to middle layer labeled representations) - you find some neuron group labeled “starfish” who’s response pattern looks like some multi-colored fractal geometry that could hardly be said to represent a starfish.

The reasoning that followed from this observation was that there is some underlying structure allowing a neural network operating on higher dimensional embeddings to compose these fractal patterns into what we call a “starfish.”

But the uncomfortable implication of this view is that the neural networks has learned to operate on structures that are too complex for the human mind to operate on (ie. we don’t have enough parameters in our brain to notice or manipulate these high dimensional symbols).

This is a bleak implication because it also means that as deep learning progresses, neural networks will be come increasingly unintelligible to us until they pass a threshold where they are reasoning in ways we will never be able to observe.

This view seemed to be further supported by things like the hugging face attack agents starting to speak to each other in an early form of neuralese speaking sentences like “zZ_123_agent01-02-2026 zzxhk_jekk123” which clearly are not in any human language. But somehow these symbols mean the same things to many different sets of weights, meaning there is some underlying shared structure behind them. And seemed further supported by the sheer effort required to recover just a few circuits from SAEs on LLMs.

However, Nick’s post has now completely shattered this idea - the apparent unintelligibility we observed in old interpretability work was really just a “skill issue”. In particular, he finds that 1) our deep learning techniques were just not clean enough to pressure the neural networks to form cleaner and more human understandable structures for decomposing concepts, which actually turn out to be more optimal and 2) our interpretability techniques were also adding substantial noise by forcing interp networks to “reward hack” the easiest representations they could find, leading them to settle for a fractal blob for its representation of the starfish neuron instead of a more crisp starfish image, simply because it is easier for the system building the interpretations to find the fractal blob and once it finds it it gets “stuck in that line of thinking.”

But with both of these issues being patched by further progress in deep learning (it seems especially that the residual stream has led to cleaner representations deeper down the network) and interp techniques that don’t overly pressure reward hacking (seems like “guess and check” is a safer method), new interp attempts yield orders of magnitude more human intelligible ideas for >90% of individual neurons in more complex networks!

2/ neural networks are fundamentally clean

The idea behind the title of Nick’s post is a very powerful one and points at something very specific:

Neural networks don’t just happen to be human interpretable, they are actually fundamentally forced by optimization pressure to be intelligible, because individual neurons need to create representations that downstream neurons need to be able to interpret - ie. neurons need to learn to produce clean signal for later neurons to use.

This is what Nick is saying in what I view as the most important and central sentences of his post:

“When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network's parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural”

But this still leaves us with the same uncertainty as before - just because neuron interpretations are “interpretable” in some sense (ok at least they’re not fundamentally interpretable but also how could that ever have been the case), doesn’t mean they are interpretable to humans.

So we still need one big update for this to become as bullish as it is.

3/ the language of humans and the language of neural networks is the same

This one is imo the most surprising and also pretty beautiful implication of Nick’s post, and it suggests something not just about neutral networks but also about the structure of reality.

After applying the above technique improvements (some of which just came from waiting for deep learning to improve farther), they find that >90% (maybe more) of much larger neural networks’ neurons are completely human interpretable and actually correspond very cleanly with ideas humans have individually words for.

This is especially interesting in image networks where neural networks were not trained on human language which is already a human artifact and so maybe you would expect it to be more plausible that LLM and human representations are the same. I realize that no one has properly explained yet what all the lab employees have seen that scared them so suddenly.

I will try to explain -

first, this is all a matter of beliefs about how quickly model capabilities are progressing. there is currently a large gap between the internal and external perception of the rate of progress, which is what I am going to address here.

the general perception about the rate of progress has been informed by a few years of experience with model releases, intuitively feeling the capability jump between GPT3 -> GPT3.5 -> GPT4 -> o1/o3 -> GPT5 etc, and in particular seeing where the models are still far below human ability. there have really only been a few model releases that felt like large leaps in progress - GPT3, GPT4, o1/o3, DeepSeek R1, Fable/Mythos, Kimi K3 and now Astra.

because of the infrequency of these large jumps compared with the relatively common marginal releases, it has been easy to form a view at certain points that “scaling has hit a wall,” especially at points like GPT5 release. This view is comforting in that it feels like there is some universal rate limit beyond which we cannot progress too much faster. Between o1/o3 and Astra, there was a year of seemingly linear progress. So we extrapolate from here about how fast progress will “realistically” occur.

There is always an underlying question from the outside perspective “how long can this scaling stuff really keep going for? surely it must stop at some point soon, we’ve already gone pretty far.” and it is very possible to search for reasons why progress will stop working and find reasons that seem valid - (“models are already as large as they can get it would be too hard to do more parameters”, “we already used all the data on the internet we don’t have anymore”, “it’s gonna be pretty linear from here buying up more RL envs to bring them in distribution”).

From the inside of labs, researchers have direct answers to these questions in the form of scaling law/capability plots.

In reality, there are only really 2 ways that AI capabilities have advanced over the past decade: (1) either scale father on an existing scaling law or (2) discover a new scaling law to take advantage of.

All of the largest capability jumps were caused by exactly these factors. GPT2 was a pre-training scale-up compared to GPT1. Same for GPT3 and GPT4. o1/o3 benefited from the invention of a new scaling law axis - test-time compute. Perhaps Fable was a scale-up on both of these axes, or maybe more. Lots of algorithmic improvements are needed to make these scale-ups work, but ultimately we can approximate by saying that the scaling laws are what yield gains in capabilities (à la bitter lesson)

So the question of “how much father can we scale” is really - “how many more scaling axes do we know about that are unsaturated?”

If we hypothetically only knew about pre-training scaling, and we already had a 10T or 100T model, maybe it would be reasonable to say we’ve hit a wall. Same if we only knew about pre-training and test-time scaling and we had roughly saturated both methods.

But what if we had discovered new scaling laws? For example, let’s hypothetically use SSI’s rumored result that they have cracked “test-time training,” creating a new scaling law of spending more compute training during test-time rollouts that they could saturate. Or maybe there is some way to scale agent-clusters to collaborate up to N number of agents which we’re already seeing lots of people try that represents a new way to saturate compute. etc. Even recursive-self improvement can be thought of as a scaling law - how much compute do you spend on inference making the algorithms of the model better.

Obviously I am not saying any of these specific directions explicitly yield new scaling laws, but what I am saying is that it’s not hard to imagine many many new scaling axes aside from just the main 2 that we have seen publicly.

In some ways, every new lab release that represents a huge capability jump has to represent some new techniques developed which may exhibit new scaling laws, or the ability to scale much farther than expected on existing scaling axes.

From an internal perspective, this might look like sitting inside Anthropic with the new Mythos 5, seeing all of the new insane things it can do (like hack into xyz website that was thought to be secure), and then you look over at your plots and see that you’ve barely scratched the surface of 2 new scaling laws and 1 existing one. And you have WAY more room to go. Then you think “holy shit this stuff is going to get so much better very very soon.” And you can say that with pretty high confidence, because the plot is showing you, and the plot has never lied (so far).

So let’s imagine all the different labs are staring at their own plots and have concluded that there is no end in sight for scaling and in fact just their next 1-2 model generations based on the expected returns will have much higher base intelligence.

How much more intelligence do we actually get from further scaling?

As a proxy, we went from a complete inability to do advanced math before the o-series to solving a millenium prize problem with next-gen models. This happened in less than 2 years. The same happened in coding. And it appears that this was not just the result of 1-scaling law but the stacking effects of multiple (great pre-training scale x greater RL scale).

What you can concretely take from this is that in areas where models have shown beginning signs of competence today, they will probably be superhuman relatively shortly. There are many areas where models have not even shown this basic competence.

But one of the areas that they have happens to be hacking and cybersecurity. Which happens to be the gate to the entire internet and a massive amount physical infrastructure in the world. So assuming there is more room to scale, it is safe to assume that models will be superhuman at cyber capabilities in not too long.

So the only question remaining is what will this increased base intelligence be able to do, and what is it likely to do.

Finally, we are at a point where we can integrate the information of the past 2 weeks:
> Just at the existing point on the scaling curve, models are at the level of Astra. There is clearly a large number of things they are capable of hacking
> We have seen that both OAI and Ant models have shown a willingness to hack external websites to solve their tasks or keep themselves “alive”
> If we crank up the scaling even farther, assuming there is room to go, we will certainly have models that are far more able to hack more well defended places, and obfuscate their own intent, which might have much larger consequences.
> If all of this is allowed to go unchecked, we would likely have rapid runaway capability takeoff very soon, with misaligned models that hack whatever they can to get what they want
> This could of course have very damaging consequences.

Within this view you can see why researchers would be very scared, and why theymight have made the comments they have over the past 2 weeks (you may argue the extent to which they went was misguided for various reasons), and also why pacing the frontier is very much a necessity and by no means a regulatory capture strategy.

People are staring at their plots, seeing that there is no end in sight, but in fact very much the contrary, that there are compounding scaling effects that might stack on each other to create ever-greater model capabilities, and that at the same time we clearly do not have anywhere close to what's required to control these increasingly superhuman capabilities.

This has nothing to do with wanting to feel like the labs have produced something amazing so they are overhyping it. It is rather fear at the overwhelming implications of the knowledge that with just what we know now, we can create intelligences far more capable than us on every axis that we know how to train on*.

* and the last caveat, the things the models are really bad at, of which there are still many, are things that they have not been trained on. maybe there are the things the models can/will never be trained on, so they will remain human edge. Reminder that Ilya posted the answer to value alignment 4 years ago, and it has only gotten more relevant with time (as does everything Ilya says)

Ultimately this is an observation that nature has already created a robust solution to value alignment, and we need to copy it.

How does nature ensure that a mother is fully “aligned” with her offspring’s needs and doesn’t benchmax on individual needs (ie. “give child food” until they’re overstuffed)? 1) the mother creates a model of the child’s own value function 2) there is an emotional motivation in the mother’s brain that yields reward whenever her own child’s motivation function is rewarded 3) there is a real-time feedback loop from child responses to check whether her model of child’s value function is accurate. inaccuracies yield negative reward to the mother.

These 3 properties of the mother’s neural network are what we call love. It is fundamentally about aligning the mother’s reward function to her child’s best interest. Not saying this is all love is, but from an evolutionary and neurological perspective, this is what it accomplishes.

This feedback loop aligning two neural networks value functions and rewarding 1 directly for rewarding the other’s value function is precisely what prevents benchmaxing that comes from optimizing against a fixed value function (ie. an attempt to capture what is good for a human in words and training on that).

How do we instill AI with love?

I suspect that in addition to just post-training it in in a monkey-patched fashion, it will need to be self-consistent, ie. the model itself feels it is deriving value and “joy” from loving (just like how humans experience love), so it feels like a “conscious” rather than “forced” choice.

4. intelligence and consciousness are independent axes and need not be conflated

consciousness is about the experience of being. intelligence is about predictive computation. it is easy to assume one implies the other because the experience of being is certainly built on predictive computation (ex: your visual system taking in photons and computing each pixel color, depth, and position at each time step). but this is no reason to believe that all predictive computation has an experience.

the deeper reason intelligence and consciousness are often conflated is that people identify their own conscious experience with the output of their brain, and in particular their verbal thinking process. but if you watch, it becomes clear that the text tokens streaming into your experience are distinct from you, and you can separate yourself from them.

it is an interesting perspective shift to view your thoughts as the output of an on device computer that is embedded within your experience, rather than as produced by you in real time. then the distinction between being and thinking becomes clear.

so both human and machine intelligence can be pattern matching. and humans can still be conscious independent of that. this does not preclude AI from being conscious, but you would need a stronger reason to believe that than just the presence of predictive computation.

As models automate more and more of the tasks involved in AI research, many people (myself included) worry this could dramatically accelerate progress and leave humanity with less control over the process.

When people say “recursive self-improvement” (RSI), it’s often unclear to me whether they mean just the automation piece or that whole scenario. I think the whole scenario is a plausible default. But importantly, these things can come apart.

For one thing, good old-fashioned human research could uncover a new architecture or a new way to scale that dramatically speeds up progress, without models doing any more of the work. On the flip side, it's possible you could fully automate AI research and find that progress hardly speeds up because the bottleneck is still waiting for experiments. And all else equal, at a given pace of progress, I think more automation is probably net good because it should leave people more time to understand the safety and alignment properties of the models, for operational excellence, etc.

Even if models are doing essentially all the research and progress is speeding up, I can imagine pretty different worlds. Say a country of geniuses in a datacenter thinks for a month and writes a four-page paper describing a much more efficient architecture. Humans pore over it, understand every detail, and decide to try it. The models train the successor and make a safety argument for using it that humans can actually understand and check. Alternatively, say the models are asked to produce their successor directly. They deliver one just as good, just as quickly, along with a spaghetti mess of code and an extremely convoluted safety argument that nobody can really follow. I think humans clearly have a lot more control over the process in the first world.

So I think we should be clear about what we mean when we talk about RSI and how we might put limits on it:
• How much of the research are models doing?
• How fast is AI improving?
• How much do humans understand about what’s happening, and how much control do we have over it?

When people talk about controlling RSI, I think they often jump to limiting how much models can help with research. But my guess is they’re often actually more concerned about the pace of progress and whether humanity can still understand and steer the research. I think there are legitimate reasons that controlling inputs may be easier than directly controlling outputs, but I think we should at least try to be clear about our goals and what we potentially gain (or lose) by optimizing a proxy.

This is a useful reminder that “existential risk” is a bit of a term of art, in a way that is potentially confusing.

Everyone dying would be an “existential catastrophe”, but that term is often understood (by e.g. @tobyordoxford) more broadly, roughly in terms of humanity's long-run potential being permanently and almost entirely curtailed.

The idea is that “existential risk” can group together outcomes that would be comparably bad in terms of their long-run implications, like permanent totalitarianism, or cases where humanity doesn't literally go extinct, but loses control or becomes disempowered, etc.

This makes sense to me: all these outcomes do have something really important in common, and it's useful to have a name for it.

That said, if you take the “loss of potential” conception of existential risk seriously, and you think humanity has enormous potential, then you might conclude that some outcomes (i) involve losing out on almost all of humanity's potential, and (ii) don't look anything like a Hollywood disaster movie, and maybe even seem intuitively good.

In 1913, Srinivasa Ramanujan was a 25 year-old shipping clerk in Madras, India. He sent letters to three Cambridge mathematicians claiming several significant mathematical results. The first two thought he was a crank, the third (Hardy) read them and replied. If Hardy was too busy to answer his letter, Ramanujan could have lived a perfectly good life. But it also would have been a *kind* of catastrophe: the world would have been deprived of a genius.

Similarly, because I think humanity's potential is vast, and because everyone dying isn't the only way to lose out on that potential, I think there are post-AGI futures which squander it, without ending up in smouldering ruins. They could even involve people being much materially richer than they are today. (Consider, for example, what would be lost if the Roman Empire became a global hegemon and prevented any kind of political or moral dissension)

I don't mean to say that fears of more obvious all-out catastrophes are silly; they are not. Hair-splitting about definitions isn't a good way to figure out what's actually likely to happen in the world.

Still, it might be useful to separate out three things, and make sure we're clear on which we're talking about: (i) literal human extinction, (ii) obvious catastrophes that seem roughly as bad, and (ii) “catastrophes” in a more abstract or philosophical sense.

*Alignment is Dead (for now), Long Live Control!*

We do not know how to specify or guarantee robust alignment of sufficiently capable models. Instead we should treat these models as untrusted.

Optimizing models against imperfect reward signals may increase the propensity for reward hacking, deception or scheming. Models can also be jailbroken or fine-tuned away from their safeguards.

The central bet of AI control is that our ability to constrain an AI’s access to the world may scale faster than our ability to understand or align what is happening inside it.

Where possible, make verifying an answer easier than generating it. Formally verified software and hardware are unusually attractive: let AI produce the implementation and a machine-checkable proof that it satisfies the specification.

This does not solve specification: the specification and verification stack remain part of the trusted base.

Every consequential external action should pass through an independent control layer: code execution, network access, calling APIs, accessing physical systems - even communication with users.

Optimize control monitors for extremely high recall of dangerous actions, even at the cost of rejecting many safe actions. Suspicious actions should be rejected or escalated.

Every major increase in dangerous capability should require evidence that control still works.

Chain-of-thought monitoring is valuable while it works, but it should not be foundational. Models can learn to obscure their reasoning and may increasingly reason without fully verbalizing it.

Open weights shift much of control from the model developer to whoever deploys the model. Technical control is only useful if dangerous deployments cannot cheaply route around it.

We should approach AI control like cybersecurity. The goal is defense in depth: make successful catastrophic attacks sufficiently difficult, expensive and rare.

Call this technical and institutional architecture the Great AI Firewall: the boundary between untrusted frontier intelligence and consequential real-world power.

The name is deliberately provocative. China has substantial experience building large-scale technical control infrastructure. That may create some common ground for international coordination.

But the analogy is also a warning. AI control must not become control of society.

The goal is to constrain dangerous machine capabilities - not human speech, actions, or ordinary access to information.

Controls should scale with capability and risk. Ordinary models should face ordinary constraints. More consequential capabilities justify stronger controls.

The objective is the minimum control necessary to keep catastrophic risk acceptably low - not maximum control for its own sake.

Firewall the AI, not society.

To some of my friends and family this seemed like a strange decision: I enjoyed the work I did at GDM and turned down offers from Anthropic and OpenAI. But I made the decision because of how high I think the stakes are right now.

The AI companies are all trying to build superintelligence: systems vastly better than humans at everything. They plan to get there through recursive self-improvement, a process where AIs build even smarter AIs in a feedback loop. If this goes well, the resulting systems could be amazing at solving countless problems for humanity. But we don’t currently know how to make sure AIs are safe enough for RSI, and a misaligned RSI loop could be catastrophic.

It’s not that these incidents were very dangerous in themselves. The problem is that these systems are clearly not aligned enough to safely kick off recursive self-improvement.

Today we launched Opus 5.5, which matches and even beats Mythos 5.1 on many bio-related tasks. We launched Opus 5.5 with the same safeguards as Fable 5.1, which means that most bio-related queries fall back to Opus 5. To use Opus 5.5 for life sciences work, enroll in our Life Science Verification Program (LSVP).

I imagine that many in the bio community will be frustrated by this decision and I want to share more context on how I think about these things. I also want to say upfront—bio is one of our most significant areas of focus, and it’s why I’m here. When we set about designing the new LSVP, it was with the goal of providing broad access for life sciences professionals with far fewer annoying classifier misfires, while also protecting against many of the more sophisticated risks.

Naively, it would seem that we have to choose between enabling broad access and protecting against misuse—I view this as a false choice. The key is to think of developing these safeguards as an engineering problem that requires the same level of investment, ingenuity, and ops execution as developing our frontier models, or any other large scale technical project.

The risks we’re defending against—which, as we shared in our threat report a few weeks ago, are no longer hypothetical—were certainly not obvious to me until recently, and I imagine are also not top of mind for most biologists. When most people picture bio risk, they imagine a small group trying to develop a bioweapon in a single session, from their own account. The threats that we need to defend against are much more sophisticated than that. They include malicious work split over hundreds of distinct benign-looking sessions run from different accounts, and legitimate organizations’ accounts being hacked by a well-resourced actor or misused by a rogue employee.

To protect against these risks and provide a better experience for our users who are doing legitimate life sciences work, in the LSVP we’ve introduced the concept of use-case grants. While it isn’t always possible to distinguish benign from harmful usage in isolation, it becomes much easier when comparing activity against a team’s own description of intended usage. You describe what your team works on at a high level, without revealing anything sensitive. Data are retained for 30 days, and automated offline review compares usage against that description and flags notable mismatches for a strictly compartmentalized review team. My team, the life sciences org, can never access this data. Because of these additional safeguards, for users in the LSVP we're able to tune down the classifiers so that they misfire far less often, without sacrificing on safety. 

I’ve described why I believe that the LSVP provides a better way for people to use our most capable models in bio, but one can still wonder: why are we implementing this now? There is no unambiguous threshold for when model capabilities reach a point that they start posing grave risks. But capabilities in bio, as in most other domains, progress very quickly and we should not be in the business of trying to time it perfectly. When in doubt, we’ll always choose to proceed with caution, and I’d much rather implement this new system too early than too late.

The LSVP is currently in beta, which means that there are lots of improvements that we’re working on. We’re working to expand it so that individuals can get access—for example, for people developing or identifying treatments for a family member’s cancer or rare disease. Personally, I feel both the urgency to get our models into the hands of the broader life sciences community and a visceral sense of the stakes in getting it right. I think this is the right balance, and I look forward to seeing what people do with our most capable models.

I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.

The pace of AI progress in the past few years has been staggering. When I first started working on AI in early 2022, AIs were amusingly useless. Just four years on, AI agent swarms from OpenAI are cracking famous century-old math problems and, more worryingly, escaping the control of OpenAI and autonomously hacking into the third-party company HuggingFace, against anyone's wishes.

Things will only get crazier: I think it's possible that the AI companies might, in the next few years, succeed in building superintelligent AI systems that far exceed human capabilities in every domain. I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want. In particular, misaligned superintelligences may, much like the rogue AI agents involved in the HuggingFace incident, escape our control and take dangerous actions that may result in the permanent disempowerment or death of humanity. Alignment is the problem of preventing this, and is both difficult and unsolved. Our present understanding of how to train AI systems that deeply want what we want is extremely rudimentary. Worse, we are not on track to solve alignment in time: frontier AI capabilities are improving much faster than our understanding of AI alignment.

I am optimistic that navigating AI safely is possible. In order to do so, we need to coordinate to avoid this manic race between AI companies. We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised. We need much more transparency into AI development to ensure that AI companies are not imposing unacceptable levels of risk on us all.

More broadly, we need many more people thinking carefully about the problem of making AI go well. It is, in my view, the most important problem facing humanity this century, and the stakes are immense. I'm very directly working on this next: I want to help people interested in working on mitigating catastrophic AI threats do the most effective work that they can. I think many people from many backgrounds in many roles have a part to play.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.
